title: Reading the prophets; the accents as a tradition

objectives.can: Read a prophetic oracle: messenger formula, direct address, word-play and imagery; and use the accents as a record of how the tradition phrased the verse.

explanation.summary: A prophetic oracle is a message delivered in the name of the one who sent it. It has its own markers: a formula that opens the message, a cry that opens a woe, a word that turns from accusation to announcement. Prophetic poetry also plays on sound and uses vivid images. This lesson also looks at the accents as a tradition of how the verse was phrased, and says how much weight they carry.

sections.heading: The marks of an oracle
body: A prophet speaks as a messenger. The formula כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה, 'thus says the LORD', is the form of a messenger delivering the words of the one who sent him. In Amos 5:4 it stands before the message, כִּי כֹה אָמַר יְהוָה לְבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל, and the words that follow are the sender's, not the prophet's own.

Other markers help the reader. The phrase נְאֻם יְהוָה, 'the declaration of the LORD', marks words as the LORD's own utterance. It often closes a sentence, as in Amos 2:11. The cry הוֹי opens an oracle of woe, as in Amos 5:18 and Isaiah 5:8. It is a cry of grief or alarm that is then followed by a description of those it is aimed at. And לָכֵן, 'therefore', usually turns from the charge to the announcement that follows from it, as in Amos 5:11, 5:13 and 5:16.

Where
What it does
rows: Opens a message delivered in the name of the sender
Marks the words as the LORD's declaration
A cry of grief or alarm that opens a woe oracle

sections.heading: Direct address and plural imperatives
body: Prophetic speech is full of commands to a group. Isaiah 40:1 begins with a doubled plural imperative, נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ, 'comfort, comfort', and the following verses pile up more of them: דַּבְּרוּ, קִרְאוּ, פַּנּוּ, יַשְּׁרוּ. The text does not say who is being addressed. A voice speaks to an unnamed group, and then another voice speaks in 40:6, so the reader should note the speaker as well as the address.

The repetition of an imperative is a way of giving it weight. 'Comfort, comfort' does not ask for two acts but for urgency. The speaker is named at the end of the verse: יֹאמַר אֱלֹהֵיכֶם, 'your God says', and עַמִּי, 'my people', shows that the speaker is the LORD.

sections.heading: Word-play and imagery
body: Prophets often play on sound. In Isaiah 5:7 the poet says that he looked for מִשְׁפָּט and saw מִשְׂפָּח, and that he looked for צְדָקָה and saw צְעָקָה. The two words in each pair sound almost alike and mean different things; the near-match carries the charge. In Amos 5:5, הַגִּלְגָּל גָּלֹה יִגְלֶה, the name of the place sounds like the verb 'go into exile', and the doubling of the verb (an infinitive absolute and a yiqtol) makes the statement emphatic: 'Gilgal will surely go into exile.' A translation can seldom keep such a play, so notice it in the Hebrew.

The images are also parallel, as in the earlier lessons. In Amos 5:24, וְיִגַּל כַּמַּיִם מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה כְּנַחַל אֵיתָן, the verb of the first line serves the second, and the second line sharpens the image: justice like water, and righteousness like a stream that never dries. In Isaiah 40:6–8 the grass and the flower, which wither, are set against the word of our God, which stands.

sections.heading: The accents as a tradition
body: The signs placed above and below the words of the text are called accents. They were written down by the Masoretes in the early Middle Ages from a tradition of reading aloud that is older. They do two things at once. They mark the stress of each word and a melody for chanting the verse, and they show how the tradition grouped the words: which words go together and where the pauses fall. The main pause in a verse is the atnah, and the verse closes with the silluq.

The accents are therefore an early interpretation of the verse, and they deserve weight, since they preserve how generations of readers phrased it. They are not infallible. A reader weighs them against the sense, the parallel lines and, where they exist, the ancient translations. When the accents divide a verse differently from the way you would, ask why before you overrule them.

There are two accent systems. The three poetic books, Psalms, Proverbs and Job, have their own system. The other twenty-one books, including Isaiah and Amos, have the prose system, even where the text is poetry. Many signs are shared, but their names and the ranking of the pauses differ.

Look at what the atnah does in these verses. In Amos 5:4 it stands on יִשְׂרָאֵל and cuts the formula from the message: 'thus says the LORD to the house of Israel' // 'seek me and live'. In Isaiah 40:1 it stands on עַמִּי and sets 'your God says' apart. In Isaiah 40:2 it stands on עֲוֺנָהּ, grouping the first two כִּי clauses (her service is complete, her iniquity is paid) and leaving the third, 'she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins', as a line by itself.

head: Books
Accent system
rows: The other twenty-one books, such as Isaiah and Amos, including their poetry

misunderstandings: The formula 'thus says the LORD' does not mean that the prophet is giving his own opinion. It is the form of a messenger delivering a message, and the sender is the one who 'says'.
Plural imperatives do not name their addressees. Do not fill the gap from memory: read who the text says is speaking and what it says.
The accents are not punctuation in the modern sense. They show stress, melody and grouping together, and a reader may weigh their grouping against the sense.
The accents are neither worthless nor infallible. They are an early and weighty interpretation, to be checked, not obeyed blindly and not ignored.

deeper.heading: Two accent systems
body: The poetic system of Psalms, Proverbs and Job and the prose system of the other books share many signs, but they rank them differently and name some of them differently. That is why the same sign may stand for a different degree of pause in Psalm 1 and in Isaiah 40. Wickes described the system of the twenty-one prose books in one treatise and the poetic books in another.

deeper.heading: Chant and sense
body: Today's chanting traditions differ between communities and are not the accents themselves, which are signs in the text. What the signs share is a grouping of the words. When two readings of a verse are possible, the accents show which one the tradition chose, and that is the use to make of them in a lesson like this.

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A doubled plural imperative, נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ, 'comfort, comfort', for an unnamed group, and the object עַמִּי, 'my people'. The atnah stands on עַמִּי, so the tradition sets יֹאמַר אֱלֹהֵיכֶם, 'your God says', apart as the closing line. The speaker is the one who calls the people 'my people'.

quoted.title: Amos
quoted.english: For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel: Seek ye Me, and live;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The messenger formula כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה opens the message, introduced by כִּי, 'for'. The atnah on יִשְׂרָאֵל cuts the introduction (to the house of Israel) from the message itself, the two imperatives דִּרְשׁוּנִי וִחְיוּ, 'seek me and live'. The accent matches the structure of the oracle.

quoted.title: Amos
quoted.english: Therefore thus saith the LORD, the God of hosts, the Lord: Lamentation shall be in all the broad places, and they shall say in all the streets: 'Alas! alas!' and they shall call the husbandman to mourning, and proclaim lamentation to such as are skilful of wailing.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: לָכֵן turns to the announcement, and the full messenger formula is lengthened by the titles of the LORD, אֱלֹהֵי צְבָאוֹת. The wail הוֹ הוֹ, 'alas, alas', is quoted from the mourners, and the verse is about mourning in the squares and streets.

quoted.title: Amos
quoted.english: But let justice well up as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two lines divided by the atnah on מִשְׁפָּט. The verb וְיִגַּל serves both lines, and each line has a simile: כַּמַּיִם and כְּנַחַל אֵיתָן. The second line sharpens the image of water by making it a stream that never dries. This is parallelism in prophecy, as in the Psalms.

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah the plant of His delight; and He looked for justice, but behold violence; for righteousness, but behold a cry.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two word-plays in one verse: מִשְׁפָּט and מִשְׂפָּח, and צְדָקָה and צְעָקָה. Each pair sounds almost alike. The poet says that the LORD looked for the first of the pair and saw the second. The Hebrew sound carries the charge, which a translation seldom keeps.

reading.why: A prophetic comfort oracle with the markers of the lesson: plural imperatives with an unnamed addressee (40:1–3), two voices (40:3 and 40:6), imagery of levelled land and withering grass (40:4, 40:6–8), and an antithetic close (40:8). Each verse also shows an atnah, so you can see how the tradition grouped it.

segments.title: Isaiah
segments.english: Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God.

segments.title: Isaiah
segments.english: Bid Jerusalem take heart, and proclaim unto her, that her time of service is accomplished, that her guilt is paid off; that she hath received of the LORD'S hand double for all her sins.

segments.title: Isaiah
segments.english: Hark! one calleth: 'Clear ye in the wilderness the way of the LORD, make plain in the desert a highway for our God.

segments.title: Isaiah
segments.english: Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill shall be made low; and the rugged shall be made level, and the rough places a plain;

segments.english: And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together; for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it.'

segments.english: Hark! one saith: 'Proclaim!' And he saith: 'What shall I proclaim?' 'All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field;
